title: War—What Is It Good For?
gist: Teaser excerpt (paywalled after two paragraphs; content does not yet address war despite the title): Louis-Vincent Gave revisits Beat Notz's rule to buy German bunds and US stocks in turmoil, arguing the Bundesbank's bondholder-protector role has passed via the ECB's ascendancy to the People's Bank of China, leaving Chinese government bonds as the only credible store-of-value bond market.

themes.theme: Notz crisis rule: bunds and US stocks

insights.claim: Beat Notz's long-standing crisis heuristic, as relayed by Louis-Vincent Gave, holds that the German Bundesbank protects bondholders while US policymakers protect equity holders, so in market turmoil one should buy German bunds and US stocks.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A classic crisis-hedge pairing (core sovereign bonds plus US equities) rooted in which policymaker defends which asset class.
insights.quote: the German Bundesbank will always do what it can to save the bondholders, while US policymakers will bend over backwards to save the equity holders

insights.claim: US policymakers are characterized as reliably bending over backwards to rescue equity holders during market stress, implying a policy 'put' under US stocks.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Supports buying US equity drawdowns in turmoil on the expectation of policy support.

insights.claim: Louis-Vincent Gave argues the half of the Notz rule covering German bunds broke down because the Bundesbank was effectively 'murdered' by the European Central Bank, ending its role as the guardian of bondholders.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: German bunds may no longer be the reliable crisis store of value they once were under the Bundesbank.
insights.quote: the Bundesbank was murdered by the European Central Bank
insights.locator: Of course, in the years that followed

insights.claim: According to Gavekal, the bondholder-protecting role once played by the Bundesbank has been taken up by the People's Bank of China, a thesis laid out in Louis-Vincent Gave's 2019 book Clash of Empires: Currencies and Power in a Multipolar World.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Frames the PBoC as the new conservative, bondholder-friendly central bank, relevant to reserve and safe-haven allocation.
insights.locator: Of course, in the years that followed

insights.claim: Gavekal concludes that Chinese government bonds are now the only credible 'store of value' government bond market, implying they should replace German bunds in a crisis-hedge portfolio paired with US stocks.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Suggests allocating to Chinese government bonds as the defensive bond leg in turmoil instead of bunds.
insights.quote: This has left Chinese government bonds as the only credible “store of value” bond market.
insights.locator: Of course, in the years that followed
